The equation can be rearranged into other forms. The form equation (1.1.2) (1.1.2) y=mx+c is particularly useful. Here, m represents the gradient of the line and c represents the y -intercept, i.e. the point (0,c) where the line meets the y -axis (figure 1.1). Sketch of $y=mx+c$, showing that the y-coordinate of the line increases by $m$ for every distance 1 moved in the x-direction. The animation in figure 1.2 (online version only) allows you to control the gradient and intercept of a straight line with sliders. Figure 1.2: Interactive plot of a straight line. Some useful properties of straight lines, as demonstrated in figure 1.3, are as follows (a)​Two lines are parallel if they have the same gradient. For example, y=x/2+3 and y=x/2 are parallel. (b)​Two lines are perpendicular if the product of their gradients is -1 . For example, y=-3x+5 and y=x/3 are perpendicular. Note the exception is vertical lines, where the gradient is undefined. (c)​A horizontal line has equation y=c . (d)​A vertical line has equation x=d . (e)​Two lines cross at a point where they have the same value of y for a given value of x . Example 1.1.1 (DIY). Find the crossing point of the lines y=-\frac{1}{2}x+4,\qquad y=x+1. Solution (left blank for your working) Equate the two expressions for y : -\frac{1}{2}x+4=x+1. Rearranging gives 3=3x/2 , and hence x=2 . Substitution into the second equation gives y=2+1=3 . Therefore, (x,y)=(2,3). An example we have already met is the straight-line equation y=mx+c . Animplicit relation has the form equation (1.2.1) (1.2.1) f(x,y)=d\,, for some constant d . For a given value of x , there may be multiple y values that satisfy this (and vice versa). An example we have already met is the equation of a circle (x-a)^{2}+(y-b)^{2}=R^{2}. In some cases, it is not possible to write a relation explicitly as y=f(x) . For example, 4x+8y+\sin(\pi x)+\cos(\pi y)=1 , which is plotted in figure 1.7, behaves like an explicit function, with one value of y for each x , however, we cannot reformulate it as an explicit function. Refer to caption Figure 1.7: A plot of the implicit function 4x+8y+\sin(\pi x)+\cos(\pi y)=1 . Example 1.2.1 (Video). So x and y are both functions of the parameter t . For example, the equation of a circle in parametric form is given by x=a+R\cos t,\qquad y=b+R\sin t, for 0\leq t<2\pi . Express the circle with centre at (2,3) and radius 4 in parametric form. Solution (left blank for your working) In parametric form x=a+R\cos t,\qquad y=b+R\sin t. For a=2 , b=3 , and R=4 , this gives x=2+4\cos t,\qquad y=3+4\sin t, for 0\leq t<2\pi . Given x=f(t) and y=g(t) , it may or may not be possible to express y directly as a function of x . For example, consider the parametric relation x=t^{2} , y=t^{4} . It can be written as y=x^{2} . However, for all values of t , x\geq 0 (see figure 1.9). Refer to caption Figure 1.9: Comparison of the function y=x^{2} and the parametric relation x=t^{2} , y=t^{4} . A general method to write parametric equations in explicit form is: •​rearrange the equation for the independent variable in terms of the parameter, i.e. rewrite x=f(t) into t=f^{-1}(x) ; •​substitute this into the equation for the dependent variable, i.e. replace t with f^{-1}(x) in y=g(t) . Note: t=f^{-1}(x) might not be unique, so be careful not to lose valid solutions! (E.g. x=t^{2} means t=\pm\sqrt{x} ). Example 1.2.3 (Lecture). Sodium oxide ( \mathrm{Na_{2}O} ) is placed in water producing sodium hydroxide: \mathrm{Na_{2}O+H_{2}O\longrightarrow 2NaOH}. The number of \mathrm{Na_{2}O} and \mathrm{NaOH} molecules in solution at time t\geq 0 is given by x=x_{0}e^{-\alpha t}\qquad\text{and}\qquad y=2x_{0}\left(1-e^{-\alpha t}\right) respectively, where x_{0} is the initial number of molecules of \mathrm{Na_{2}O} . Write y as a function of x , noting any restrictions on their values. Solution Find substitution for t in terms of x : \underline{\phantom{e^{-\alpha t}=\frac{x}{x_{0}}}}. Substitute into equation for y : \underline{\phantom{y=2(x_{0}-x).}} x is a decreasing function of t , since t\geq 0 , the minimum and maximum x values are \underline{\phantom{0<x\leq x_{0}.}} y is an increasing function of t , the minimum and maximum y values are \underline{\phantom{0\leq y<2x_{0}.}} The straight line and the circle can both be expressed in parametric and implicit form. Straight Line •​Implicit: ax+by=p . •​Parametric: x=bt , y=\frac{p}{b}-at . •​Explicit: y=-\frac{a}{b}x+\frac{p}{b}=mx+c . Circle •​Implicit: (x-a)^{2}+(y-b)^{2}=R^{2} . •​Parametric: x=a+R\cos t , y=b+R\sin t . •​Explicit: y=b\pm\sqrt{R^{2}-(x-a)^{2}} . Recap Key points from section 1.2 •​An explicit relation expresses the dependent variable as a function of the independent variable (e.g. y=f(x) ). •​An implicit relation expresses the relationship between the variables via a function of both, (e.g. f(x,y)=0 ). •​A parametric relation expresses the variables as functions of a parameter (e.g. x=f(t) and y=g(t) ). 1.3 Partial fractions Learning Outcomes On completion of this subsection, students will be able to •​Simplify proper and improper compound fractions into partial fractions form 1.3.1 Partial fractions in general What do we mean by “partial fractions”? Consider the following sum of two fractions: \frac{1}{x+1}+\frac{3}{x-2}. We can put them over a common denominator to express as a single fraction (see figure 1.10): \frac{4x+1}{(x+1)(x-2)}. Partial fraction decomposition is about reversing this operation. This is often useful for differentiation and integration. Refer to caption Figure 1.10: Plots of the irreducible fractions \frac{1}{x+1} + and \frac{3}{x-2} and their sum, equivalent to \frac{4x+1}{(x+1)(x-2)} . Useful definitions: •​A rational fraction has a numerator and denominator that are both polynomials. •​The degree of a polynomial is the largest power in the polynomial, e.g. x^{3}+x^{2}-x+1=0 is degree 3. •​Defining d as the degree of the denominator and n as the degree of the numerator, then a proper fraction is a rational fraction where d>n . An improper fraction is a rational fraction where d\leq n . 1.3.2 Partial fractions for proper fractions Case 1: Linear function divided by factorising quadratic. A linear function divided by a factorising quadratic can be written in the form \frac{\text{linear}}{(x-a)(x-b)}=\frac{A}{x-a}+\frac{B}{x-b}\,. To find A and B , first multiply both sides by the denominator (x-a)(x-b) to yield \text{linear}=A(x-b)+B(x-a). This equation must hold for all x . So, set x=a to find A (in terms of a , b , and the linear function) and set x=b to find B (in terms of a , b , and the linear function). Example 1.3.1 (Lecture). Express in partial fractions form \frac{x-4}{2x^{2}+5x-3}. Solution Factorise the denominator 2x^{2}+5x-3=\underline{\phantom{(x+3)(2x-1)}}. Write the form of the solution \frac{x-4}{(x+3)(2x-1)}=\underline{\phantom{\frac{A}{x+3}+\frac{B}{2x-1}}}. Multiply through by the denominator x-4=\underline{\phantom{A(2x-1)+B(x+3)}}. Solve for A and B Substituting x=-3 gives -7=-7A , therefore A=1 Substituting x=1/2 gives -7/2=-7B/2 , therefore B=-1 and so \frac{x-4}{2x^{2}+5x-3}=\underline{\phantom{\frac{1}{x+3}-\frac{1}{2x-1}}}. Case 2: Quadratic function divided by a factorising cubic. A quadratic function divided by a factorising cubic can be written in the form \frac{\text{quadratic}}{(x-a)(x-b)(x-c)}=\frac{A}{x-a}+\frac{B}{x-b}+\frac{C}{% x-c}\,. To find A , B and C , multiply through by the denominator: \text{quadratic}=A(x-b)(x-c)+B(x-a)(x-c)+C(x-a)(x-b). Then set x=a to find A , x=b to find B , and x=c to find C . Case 1 and 2 generalise to any proper fraction with linear factors on the denominator: equation (1.3.1) (1.3.1) \frac{\text{degree }n-1\text{ polynomial}}{(x-x_{1})(x-x_{2})\cdots(x-x_{n})}=% \frac{A_{1}}{x-x_{1}}+\frac{A_{2}}{x-x_{2}}+\cdots+\frac{A_{n}}{x-x_{n}}. Solution The denominator contains 3 linear factors, so the correct form is \frac{2x^{2}+8x+18}{x(x+2)(x-3)}=\underline{\phantom{\frac{A}{x}+\frac{B}{x+2}% +\frac{C}{x-3}}}. Multiplying both sides by the denominator: \underline{\phantom{2x^{2}+8x+18=A(x+2)(x-3)+Bx(x-3)+Cx(x+2)}}. Although written in implicit form, it can be differentiated. It is important to know which variable we are differentiating with respect to. In this case, we want to find {\rm d}y/{\rm d}x . Differentiate term-by-term with respect to x : •​The derivative of x^{2} is 2x •​Using the chain rule, the derivative of y^{2} is 2y\frac{{\rm d}y}{{\rm d}x} •​The derivative of 25 is zero Therefore, we have 2x+2y\frac{{\rm d}y}{{\rm d}x}=0. Which rearranges to \frac{{\rm d}y}{{\rm d}x}=-\frac{x}{y}. This is an example of implicit differentiation. The second derivative can also be found by repeating the process. Starting with x^{2}+y^{2}=25 and differentiating we get 2x+2y\frac{{\rm d}y}{{\rm d}x}=0. •​Differentiating 2x gives 2 •​Using the product rule, differentiating 2y\frac{{\rm d}y}{{\rm d}x} gives 2\left(\frac{{\rm d}y}{{\rm d}x}\right)^{2}+2y\frac{{\rm d}^{2}y}{{\rm d}x^{2}} So, we find 2+2\left(\frac{{\rm d}y}{{\rm d}x}\right)^{2}+2y\frac{{\rm d}^{2}y}{{\rm d}x^{% 2}}=0 or \frac{{\rm d}^{2}y}{{\rm d}x^{2}}=-\frac{1+\left(\frac{{\rm d}y}{{\rm d}x}% \right)^{2}}{y}. Substituting in the result from before ( {\rm d}y/{\rm d}x=-x/y ), this reduces to \frac{{\rm d}^{2}y}{{\rm d}x^{2}}=-\frac{1}{y}-\frac{x^{2}}{y^{3}}. Alternatively, we could start with the result for {\rm d}y/{\rm d}x , i.e. \frac{{\rm d}y}{{\rm d}x}=-\frac{x}{y}. Use the quotient rule to differentiate, with u=-x and v=y , so u^{\prime}=-1 and v^{\prime}=y^{\prime} : \frac{{\rm d}^{2}y}{{\rm d}x^{2}}=\frac{u^{\prime}v-v^{\prime}u}{v^{2}}=\frac{% -y+xy^{\prime}}{y^{2}}.
